cards.front: Why does raising the temperature make an enzyme-catalysed reaction go faster at first?
cards.back: Molecules gain **kinetic energy**, so they move faster and collide with the active site more often. A larger share of those collisions has enough energy to react.
cards.hint: Compare with why sugar dissolves faster in hot tea than in cold tea.

cards.front: Why does the rate of an enzyme reaction fall to zero at very high temperatures?
cards.back: Heat breaks the weak bonds holding the **tertiary structure**, so the active site changes shape and the substrate no longer fits. This change is **denaturation**.
cards.hint: Think about what extra vibration does to the folded shape.

cards.front: Why does the rate peak and then fall at the optimum temperature?
cards.back: Below the optimum, extra collisions outweigh any damage, so the rate rises. Above it, **denaturation** outweighs the gain, so the rate falls steeply to zero.
cards.hint: Two effects of heat compete on the same graph.

cards.front: What is the optimum temperature of an enzyme?
cards.back: The **optimum temperature** is the temperature at which an enzyme's activity is highest under given conditions. It differs between enzymes; many human enzymes work best near $37\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

cards.front: Why does cooling slow an enzyme without permanently damaging it?
cards.back: Molecules have little kinetic energy, so collisions are rare and few succeed. The **enzyme** keeps its shape, so activity returns when the mixture warms again.
cards.hint: Contrast this with what heat does to the bonds.

cards.front: How is the rate of reaction calculated from the volume of product collected over time?
cards.back: $\text{rate} = \frac{\text{volume of product}}{\text{time}}$, measured in $\mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-1}}$ when volume is in $\mathrm{cm^3}$ and time is in $\mathrm{s}$.
cards.hint: Each rate is one number divided by another.

cards.front: Catalase gives $6.0\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of oxygen in $120\,\mathrm{s}$ at 20 °C and $15.0\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ at 30 °C. How many times faster is the rate at 30 °C?
cards.back: The rates are $0.050\,\mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-1}}$ at 20 °C and $0.125\,\mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-1}}$ at 30 °C, so the rate at 30 °C is **2.5 times** greater.
cards.hint: Work out each rate first, then divide one by the other.

cards.front: Which variables must be kept constant when testing enzyme rate at several temperatures?
cards.back: **pH** (held steady with a buffer), enzyme concentration, substrate concentration, and volumes and reaction time, so that only temperature changes.
cards.hint: Think about what else in the mixture could change the rate.

cards.front: What are the steps for measuring enzyme rate across a range of temperatures?
cards.back: Mix enzyme and substrate in water baths at each temperature. Measure the product at fixed times, calculate the rate, then plot rate against temperature and join the points with a smooth curve.
cards.hint: Start with how the temperature is set before mixing.

cards.front: What is the temperature coefficient $Q_{10}$, and how is it calculated?
cards.back: $Q_{10}=\frac{\text{rate at }(T+10)}{\text{rate at }T}$, the rate at a temperature divided by the rate 10 °C lower. It is meaningful only below the optimum.
cards.hint: Compare two rates that are 10 °C apart.

cards.front: Why can the highest tested temperature not be assumed to be the true optimum?
cards.back: The optimum is known only to within the range tested. A temperature between two tested values might give a higher rate, so the peak must be read from a smooth curve.
cards.hint: Think about the gaps between the points you measured.

cards.front: Why can an enzyme from a hot-spring bacterium have a higher optimum temperature than a human enzyme?
cards.back: Each enzyme has its own **tertiary structure** and bonds, so the hot-spring enzyme keeps its active site intact at temperatures that would denature a human enzyme.
cards.hint: Think about what differs between enzymes from different organisms.

cards.front: Why is it wrong to say that heat has killed an enzyme?
cards.back: Enzymes are **molecules**, not living things, so heat denatures them rather than killing them. Denaturation changes the shape and usually cannot be reversed by cooling.
cards.hint: Consider what kind of thing an enzyme is.
